title: Starbirth over ALMA
caption: The Carina Nebula and star clusters above an ALMA antenna, Chajnantor plateau, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at ALMA, Chajnantor plateau, Chile

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Three deep-sky objects seem to shine just in front of the dish of an ALMA antenna in this single-exposure image, taken during the ESO Ultra HD Expedition. The most prominent is the reddish Carina Nebula. To its upper right is the star cluster NGC 3532, and to its upper left the cluster IC 2602.

The Carina Nebula is a large cloud of gas, mostly hydrogen, where stars have recently formed. Massive, short-lived blue stars born inside it pour out ultraviolet radiation that ionises the gas, making hydrogen glow its characteristic red. In time, supernovae and strong stellar winds will scatter the gas, leaving one or more star clusters behind, much like the two nearby.
The French astronomer Nicolas Louis de Lacaille was the first to catalogue all three, which lie in Carina, the Keel. Though they look close together in the sky, their distances differ greatly.

understand.summary: This is a single-exposure landscape photograph at the ALMA site, in visible light. The camera settings and colour processing are not published.
understand.eye: A camera exposure gathers more light than the eye, so the red glow of the Carina Nebula shows far more strongly than it would to someone on the plateau.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: IC 2602 is under 500 light-years away and NGC 3532 around 1300 light-years away, while the Carina Nebula is thought to be up to 10 000 light-years distant.
alt: A reddish nebula and two star clusters in the night sky, appearing in front of a large dish antenna.
